utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good morning. The sitting is resumed. We are still in the case of the Prosecutor against Kvocka and others. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case for good order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-30/1-A, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka, Mladjo Radic, Zoran Zigic, and Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And all members of the bar can hear me, I take it. Yes. And all the appellants also can hear me, I take it. Yes, I see them nodding. And the appearances are as before, and we may now proceed. Today is Friday. We have as our first item response by the Prosecution. 30 minutes, yes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOWICK
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President and Your Honours, my name is Kelly Howick, and I will be presenting the Prosecution's submissions on sentencing today. As counsel for the appellants Prcac, Kvocka and Radic did not directly address sentencing in their oral submissions, I will likewise not address them today but will rely on the Prosecution's written responses in our response brief. I will, however, be happy to answer any questions at the end of my time that you may have in regards to these sentences. As the appellant Zigic's counsel did raise certain issues in regards to sentencing, I will address his this morning. First of all, I would like to reiterate the crimes that Zoran Zigic has been convicted of. The appellant Zigic has been convicted for his co-perpetration within the JCE that was Omarska. This includes not only his criminal crimes but also the crimes that were committed in the furtherance of the joint criminal enterprise. In addition to the crimes committed at Omarska, the appellant Zigic also personally committed crimes at the Keraterm camp and Trnopolje camp. The appellant Zigic's crimes include four murders and 13 beatings which were so severe as to be found by the Trial Chamber to equate to torture, cruel or inhumane treatment. My colleague Mr. Re has described for you the severity of many of the crimes that the appellant has committed personally, and I will be using just a few of them to illustrate my points in response to Mr. Stojanovic's submissions. However, it's clear from the Trial Chamber that the gravity of these offences, the appropriate sentence in this case was 25 years. The Trial Chamber found no mitigating factors and reviewed the heinous gravity of the appellant's conduct in all three camps. And it's with these grievous crimes that I will now turn to the sentencing, the legal review of sentencing on appeal. It is well established that in challenging a sentence on appeal, the appellant must demonstrate an error in the Trial Chamber's exercise of discretion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOWICK
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. That the Trial Chamber erred in following the law, and also that this error is discernible. The appellant must demonstrate that the Trial Chamber went outside its discretionary framework in imposing the sentence. I will first address issues raised by the appellant's oral submissions. Second, I will address the effect if any that a possible acquittal regarding that Drago Tokmadzic murder in Keraterm could have on the sentence. Counsel for the appellant Zigic raised four main issues with regard to sentencing, the first being the amputation of the appellant's left forefinger, partial amputation; second, the effect of his surrender on sentencing; third, the alleged admissions and public display of remorse that the appellant made in his statement before the Court; and fourth, the Banovic plea and sentence. At the outset I would like to point out that the first three issues that the appellant raises were considered by the Trial Chamber. They were fully briefed, they were fully argued by all parties, and they were considered by the Trial Chamber. In regards to the partial amputation of the appellant's left forefinger, the appellant argues that the fact that his finger had been partially amputated at the time of the offences was given inadequate attention by the Trial Chamber. At trial, as on appeal, the appellant mainly raises this issue as a factual matter as a defence to his ability to perpetrate these crimes. This can be shown in the final trial brief at paragraphs 273 to 274 and his appeal brief at paragraphs 412 to 419. However, as I mentioned, this issue was clearly before the Trial Chamber and was litigated fully. In fact, during the trial at one point Judge Rodrigues asked Witness AE did it prevent him from beating other prisoners the fact that he had a bandaged hand. Witness AE responded no, by no means. He could use his other hand to beat people. This is at transcript page 4327. Numerous other victims noted in their testimony that Zigic's hand was bandaged at the time that they were beaten and tortured by him. These would be witnesses Ervin Ramic, Safet Taci, and Witness AD. As the appellant has indeed been convicted of these beatings, tortures and murders, the Trial Chamber clearly rejected the amputation of his left forefinger as a factual matter or as a defence, a complete defence to these beatings and tortures. As mitigation, the Prosecution can see no effect that this partial amputation of his finger could have on his sentence and indeed, the Trial Chamber rejected this as a factual matter. And it cannot be said that the Trial Chamber's failure to take this partial amputation into consideration in sentencing has been a discernible error. The appellant also claims on appeal, as at trial, that the Trial Chamber did not consider his surrender as a voluntary surrender in terms of mitigation of his sentence. He argues again that during the period nobody was voluntarily surrendering and the Republika Srpska was not extraditing persons to this Tribunal. The appellant raised these exact same arguments at trial and it was fully addressed by both parties and before the Chamber. The Trial Chamber noted in the judgement that in 1994, the appellant was convicted and sentenced to 15 years for murder in Banja Luka. In 1998, while he was serving this sentence for murder, he was surrendered to the Tribunal by the Republika Srpska authorities. The Trial Chamber found that due to the fact that he was in prison at the time of the surrender, it did not consider it as mitigation. The appellant's arguments regarding whether or not he would have been extradited by the Republika Srpska absent his concession to be surrendered to the Tribunal is entirely speculative and moreover, the Statute of this Tribunal under Article 29(2)(e) requires all signatories and members to cooperate with the Tribunal and the transfer or surrender of an accused to the Tribunal. The appellant Zigic was clearly in the custody of the Republika Srpska. They knew where he was. They were required to transfer him to the Tribunal. It is simply irrelevant whether the appellant himself agreed with this transfer. He also raises the fact that his murder case in Banja Luka was still on appeal and, therefore, not finalised. However, this is irrelevant to whether or not his surrender was voluntary. In a similar case, in Naletelic and Martinovic, the accused known as Stela was also serving a sentence for murder at the time of his surrender to the Tribunal, and in that case the Trial Chamber found that there was no mitigation of his sentence for his surrender. That's at the Naletelic and Martinovic Trial Chamber judgement at paragraph 757 and 761. The appellant simply has not demonstrated that the Trial Chamber made a discernible error in exercising its discretion in finding that his surrender did not amount to a mitigation of his sentence. The third point that the appellant raises is his alleged admissions and public apology that he made in his statement pursuant to Rule 84. During the trial the appellant did give a statement pursuant to Rule 84 but pursuant to this Rule, of course, he was not examined by either the Prosecution or the Trial Chamber on the content of the statement. It is the Prosecution's submission that the appellant did not make any statements which could be considered either admissions of his conduct or confessions as such that would rise to the level of mitigation of his sentence. The Trial Chamber clearly rejected the appellant's versions of the numerous events that he mentioned in his statement. I will summarise one of these supposed confessions that the appellant made in his statement. In relation to the victims Sead Car Jusufagic, the appellant claimed in his statement that he only made Car run around with a machine-gun and hit him once with his leg, and I quote from his statement: "I kicked him and that's all I did to Car." The appellant said then after kicking Car he left the camp, the Omarska camp, and went to -- or Keraterm camp, excuse me, and went to a bar and did not learn of what happened to Sead Jusufagic until he received the indictment. But contrary to the appellant's statement, the Trial Chamber convicted the appellant of the murder of Sead Jusufagic based on repeated and successive brutal beatings of the victim, not just for a kick. In the Prosecution's respectful submissions, the denial of crimes cannot be considered a confession or an admission, and the Appeals Chamber and the Trial Chamber should have and did not give any weight to these alleged confessions. The Trial Chamber committed no error in assigning this statement any weight in mitigation. The appellant has also claimed that his statement -- that in his statement he showed remorse for the victims. It is well settled in the jurisprudence that a Trial Chamber must find remorse to be sincere in order to consider it in mitigation. It is therefore within a Trial Chamber's discretion to determine whether or not the Trial Chamber believes that any expression of remorse is indeed sincere. The Prosecution has noted that the appellant did not confess to any of these crimes, to the crimes for which he had been charged and ultimately convicted. Instead, he continued to downplay his role in any abuses that he may have committed. In fact, in his statement, the appellant said: "I express my deep remorse and repentance to all who consider I wronged them in any way during the war. But I consider I didn't. Although some of my gestures may have pained them." This is at transcript page 9472. While the Trial Chamber may not have expressly mentioned this statement in the sentencing portion of the judgement, it is clear that the Trial Chamber rejected the appellant's version of events and rejected that his expressions of remorse were sincere. It was well within the Trial Chamber's discretion to assign this statement no weight. Finally, the appellant raised the issue of the Banovic plea and sentencing. The appellant essentially argues that an eight-year sentence that Banovic received for his plea agreement is in disparity with Zigic's sentence of 25 years. The Prosecution would like to reiterate that the Tribunal has no rigid sentencing scheme and many Trial and Appeals Chambers have also noted that a comparison between sentences is often misleading. More importantly, it has been noted that sentences as a result of plea agreements are especially difficult to compare. The appellant has not conceded the numerous distinguishing factors between his case and that of the Banovic plea and sentencing. First and most importantly, the scope of the criminality with which Mr. Banovic pled to and what the appellant Zigic has been convicted of is great, is greatly in disparity itself. While Banovic pled guilty to one count of persecution which was limited to his own involvement within the joint criminal enterprise at Keraterm, the appellant Zigic has been convicted not only of his personal participation but as a co-perpetrator within the joint criminal enterprise which also includes the other crimes committed within the joint criminal enterprise in Omarska. And it has to be emphasised that while Mr. Banovic pled to the crimes that he committed at Keraterm, the appellant Zigic has been convicted not only of the crimes he committed at Omarska but also the crimes he committed at Keraterm and Trnopolje over several months' duration. And importantly while Mr. Banovic was indeed a guard at the Keraterm camp which was taken into consideration as a factor and aggravation of his sentence the Trial Chamber in this case repeatedly noted that the appellant Zigic had no other purpose at the camps but to seek out victims for his beatings, tortures and murders. The Trial Chamber in the Banovic plea gave the accused full credit for his guilty plea. The judgement noted the importance of a guilty plea at this Tribunal and in sentencing generally. It noted that an admission of guilt demonstrates honesty and it is important to encourage others to come forward as well. A guilty plea contributes to the truth-finding mission of the Tribunal. It also has a public benefit in that it saves the Tribunal time and resources, and most importantly, a guilty plea relieves the victims and witnesses from the stress of testifying before their tormenters. The appellant Zigic, of course, can claim none of these important factors. The Trial Chamber in Banovic also found that he expressed sincere remorse. As I noted previously, the Trial Chamber in this case did not find that the appellant Zigic expressed remorse even -- or at most sincere remorse. The Prosecution would also like to clarify two issues in relation to what the appellant said about the cooperation of Mr. Banovic with the Prosecution. While it is true in the submissions of the Prosecution following the plea of guilty in Banovic, the Prosecution argued that he -- his cooperation did not rise to a level of substantial. The Trial Chamber in Banovic did in fact find that his cooperation was substantial, and that was considered in the sentence of eight years. The Trial Chamber found that Banovic substantially cooperated with the Prosecution based on interviews and the promise to cooperate fully in the future. In contrast, the Prosecution has never accepted that the appellant Zigic has cooperated substantially or otherwise with the Prosecution either at trial or on appeal, and this brings me to the second point that I would like to clarify. The appellant's counsel mentioned that he -- that the appellant had attempted to plead guilty on appeal. The Prosecution does not accept that the appellant ever attempted to honestly plead guilty. He merely attempted to admit a few incidents, namely the kicking of Car and the slap of Witness AK which had already been before the Trial Chamber and considered in his statement. Furthermore, pleas of guilty are considered as mitigation for the reasons in the Banovic plea. The Prosecution can see no value in an appellant who has been convicted of his crimes at trial, attempting to plead by minimising his participation on appeal. And finally, Banovic's young age of 23 was considered in mitigation, where at the time of his crimes the appellant Zigic was 33. The appellant has not demonstrated that the Banovic plea and sentence in any way assists in demonstrating that the Trial Chamber in this case abused its discretion or went outside its discretionary framework in sentencing the appellant to 25 years. And finally, the Prosecution would like to briefly address whether an acquittal of the appellant for the murder of Drago Tokmadzic in the Keraterm camp could have an effect on his overall sentence. It's the Prosecution's respectful submissions that given the severity and the repetitive nature of the appellant's conduct for which he has been convicted, the fact that he regularly entered the camps for the sole purpose of beating, torturing and murdering the detainees, and in light of the heinous gravity of the offences which would remain convictions even if the Drago Tokmadzic murder was reversed, an acquittal for his participation in this one particular crime should not affect his sentence. It is the Prosecution's submission that the sentence of 25 years was the appropriate one to describe the totality of the appellant's conduct, not only within the joint criminal enterprise of Omarska but also in relation to his personal conduct and commission of crimes in all three camps. And that it is the Prosecution's submissions that all of the appellant's grounds of appeal in regard to sentencing should be dismissed and his sentence upheld. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Guney has a question. Judge Guney, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the third point that you raised with respect to recognising culpability and remorse on the part of the accused, you -- you quoted the example of Jusufagic. Were there others? Can you tell us if there were others, and which others if those exist. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOWICK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This were numerous others -- [French translation on English channel]. I'm getting French. Sorry. The appellant did mention several others in his statement, and similarly to what he said about Car, he downplayed any involvement. In fact, for many of the crimes he completely avoided any mention of any participation in any of the crimes. There's one crime in particular that I did not mention in my statement that I could refer to, and that was in reference to Witness AK. The appellant admitted that he took money from the victim and hit him once based on a debt that he had -- that the witness -- victim had owed him previously to the war. The appellant in his statement said that hitting this victim caused him great pain as a result of his amputation and that he left the room, went outside, and chatted with Abdulah Brkic, who was another victim. This is what the appellant said in his own statement. Now, in the Trial Chamber's judgement, the Trial Chamber found that Zigic had actually taken this witness out of the camp, including several other victims and witnesses, and taken them to the "white house" where he and others proceeded to order them to sit like dogs while they were sworn at and beaten with weapons until they bled. And afterwards Zigic had made them crawl outside and wash off the blood and dirty water saying: "Pigs, wash yourself." And that's at Trial Chamber judgement paragraph 585 to 598. There was several victims. The only one that the appellant admitted hitting once was Witness AK which was obviously rejected by the Trial Chamber. And in his statement, if you would like to review it, he does mention several other victims. And I believe his statement was given on March 26 of 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Any questions? Thank you, Ms. Howick. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOWICK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, does that conclude the arguments for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, I'm behind the wall, but these are the submissions of the Prosecution in relation to all the appellants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we go now to the Defence, and I think we had decided -- did we decide to go in the order in which names were stated on the cover sheet of the judgement? That would place Kvocka first. Yes. Well, would counsel for Kvocka be the first to speak. Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, and good morning. During these 20 minutes, I will try to respond to yesterday's submissions of my learned colleagues of yesterday. I have three questions that I would like to put, and I will start from the most important one, in my judgement, and then will get as far as I can with the time permitting. First of all, I would like to deal with the question of the joint criminal enterprise or joint criminal intent. My colleagues yesterday and in their submissions, or in their response to the appeal in paragraph 531, concluded that the responsibility of Kvocka rests on his significant contribution to the realisation of abuse in Omarska and that in that sense his status of a functional equivalent of a deputy commander of the guards was not something that had any influence on this. This position which was indicated here yesterday in a certain way opens up the question of whether this form of criminal enterprise can be placed in group 2 from the judgement in the Tadic case. I think that Judge Mumba yesterday asked this question, because if there is no position of power, high position of power, which in itself contains the presumption of intent and motive, then I think we have a new issue here and that in this case we're talking about the first group of joint criminal enterprise. I know from the appeal judgement in the Tadic case, in that case the intent is required to commit a joint criminal enterprise. My learned colleagues did not deal with this matter, nor did they prove the existence of intent with Mr. Kvocka from the simple reason that the indictment is not consistent with the judgement. They claimed in the indictment that Kvocka was a commander, a deputy commander, of the camp, and had they proved their claims, then we would then come to the existence of a joint criminal enterprise based on the function of authority which presumes what I mentioned earlier. This means that they did not even try to prove premeditated intent with Kvocka for this kind of act. But I would also like to talk about motive or intent. The second group asks for the existence of this intent or motive in order to prove such an act. We believe that evidence in this case did not prove the existence of Kvocka's intent. Kvocka does not dispute that he went there of his own will. He did not go to work there voluntarily, but he went according to the schedule of his professional duties, believing for a long time that he was performing a legitimate job which in those initial days seemed quite in accordance with the rules of service public security service in conditions of exceptional circumstances, and he was a member of this extraordinary security service. However, during his stay in Omarska, which amounted to 17 days with two four-day breaks, Kvocka publicly because of his political positions and because of his personal and family circumstances and because of his professional commitment publicly demonstrated his disagreement with the policy and the events in the camp. He brought food packages there. Every time that he had the opportunity he opposed and prevented violence. He publicly brought in medicines. He criticised what was happening. And finally, the Trial Chamber itself -- because of such conduct of Kvocka's the atmosphere was much better in Omarska for as long as he was there. It was not better because he was in a position of authority but because he tried in extraordinary circumstances to do his job as much as this was possible. Of course his conduct in this sense was not something that his bosses looked upon favourably nor the people who committed these crimes. Because of that and because of his public positions and actions and public disagreement, Kvocka was dismissed from the Omarska camp on the 22nd of June, 1992, which was his last day of work there. Mr. Kvocka believed that he was transferred to the police station in Tukovi because he did not receive any other kind of information. He was just told by Simo Drljaca to hand in his weapons and to go home. However, during the evidentiary proceedings when certain documents were disclosed, Kvocka found out, learned that he had been dismissed and that he returned to Tukovi on the 1st of July based on a decision about -- which he found out for the first time once he was here in The Hague. Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, the chief of the public security centre in Banja Luka made a decision, number 11/101-6, which was tendered into evidence as D139, which states you cannot dismiss a worker without the centre for public security being informed about that, and you have to find adequate solutions in order to give them different duties which are not contrary to the rules. Item 1 of this decision points out who can work at which positions, and only due to those reasons Kvocka was not left without a job. He was taken out of Omarska because of his public disagreement with the policies conducted in Omarska. This is indicated also about the statement of Jadran Mikic, Zdravko Samardjia also, who say that Kvocka should have been tapped by Simo Drljaca because of his activities. His conversations should have been bugged. Because of distrust towards Kvocka, Lazar Basrak also spoke about that, a witness who testified and who was the assistant commander of the reserve police station in Tukovi where Kvocka was transferred following the intervention of Mr. Zupljanin on the 1st of July. I would just like to have a second to prove into a private session because Mr. Basrak spoke about this meeting during private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Agreeable? Agreeable to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. So ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Also, Your Honours, Witness F testified before the Trial Chamber, a witness who had spent the entire time in Omarska. During her testimony she said, I quote:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "You said that he, Kvocka, had lost his job. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "You said -- you told Ms. Hollis and she quoted your words. We asked why did he lose his jobs and the guards said -- -- and you said, and I'm quoting -- " -- he was good for you but he's not good for us. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "When he said he's good for you, who did they mean? Did they mean Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Yes, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "And when they said not for us, did they mean Serbs when they said "For us"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Yes, Serbs. Chetniks. Your Honours, this is the testimony of a witness before the Trial Chamber who also talked about Kvocka's dismissal and the reasons for this dismissal. I must say that also we have an affidavit on this matter, the statement by Rezak Crnalic who testified about the dismissal. Yesterday my learned friends mentioned the standard in the Krnojelac judgement where disagreement with persecutions or absence of intent would substantiate a dismissal. We would like to say that a dismissal has a more specific weight than resignation for the reason that this contains resistance, public disagreement, a showing that there is no cooperation. So for that reason, we believe that Kvocka had no intent or motive to participate or support the plan because the absence of this support resulted in his dismissal and then, in the spirit of Mr. Zupljanin's decision, it resulted in him being transferred to marginal post. The third element which we were looking at here is the obligation of the Prosecution to prove substantial contribution. First of all, we would have to define what a substantial contribution is. My learned colleague yesterday introduced a standard, the standard of relay, that it is a chain in which people pass the baton from one to the other. This was also applied in the indictment. They said Kvocka was a deputy. The moment he was taken out of Omarska a different deputy was brought in order to take over his duties, to take on himself the baton. Unfortunately we believe that the indictment was not proved; the reverse was proved. Kvocka was not the deputy, Prcac was not brought in to replace him and there was no temporal nexus in all of these events. Also, we must say, Your Honours, that by dismissing Kvocka from Omarska, nobody came to replace him. We would also like to point out to the learned Judges that during his four-day absence from the camp, nobody substituted for him. Nobody was brought in to function so that this baton and relay would function. We tried to prove and I believe that the Chamber will be convinced that Kvocka was just a member, just a cog in the machine. He was a deputy police officer as part of a 24-hour guards duties, part of the security service. And as a police officer he worked to his full abilities, and he's proud of that. He's proud that in his term of office the circumstances there were better. We state this today. He's proud because as a man, as a police officer, he made his contribution to prevent, stop, and alleviate what was happening at the camp. He could not have done more. And the result of that, that he could not have done more, was his dismissal from Omarska and all the consequences that followed. Now, I would like to go back to the question of the objections to the form of the indictment. Yesterday, we all agreed - and I spoke about this on Wednesday - that the indictment was not really reflected in the judgement at all. Responding to Judge Weinberg de Roca's question, and this was confirmed by the Prosecution yesterday also, the fact in itself that there is no identity between the indictment and the judgement opens up the serious question of the right of to a fair trial. This is all a scholastic debate. We're all intelligent people. We could have assumed certain things, but we did not assume anything here. The Prosecution was there to prosecute, to make their case, to inform us about it and to prove it, especially because the institute of the joint criminal enterprise was mentioned for the first time in the opening statement and that it represents an integral part of the indictment. There is no case before the Tribunal except for this one where this was not incorporated into the indictment. Responding to a remark by our colleagues that we did not object to that, we were simply not able to do this. The opening statement actually -- and the first time we were able to address that was actually in the closing statement, and we did object to this and we did say that we were prevented from responding to this matter in an adequate manner. And I still have time for my third question, and that is the matter of factual errors. Again, I would like to start from matters that we all agreed on. There is no identity between the indictment and the judgement. The indictment was drafted by the Prosecution based on what? Based on hundreds of statement witnesses, based on hundreds and thousands of documents, based on an expert, learned analysis with which evidence it can prove its claims. And what happened? The evidence that they submitted, that evidence brought before the Trial Chamber did not confirm the case that they were making. There is no consistency between the evidence, the claims or the charges in the indictment, and the judgement. When we're talking about Kvocka's status, the functional equivalent of a deputy of the guards service, we believe that also in this case there is no consistency between the conclusion of the Trial Chamber with the evidence that the Trial Chamber relies on. And of course this is not possible. This cannot be, absolutely. Because my learned friends did not make the case that Kvocka was the equivalent functional I don't know what, but they claimed that he was a commander and they brought people who claimed that he was a commander. They brought witnesses who said that Kvocka was deputy commander. They brought people who were telling a different story. And based on that story, the conclusion was to be drawn that Kvocka was a functional equivalent. If you compare the statements of these witnesses, then we can see that this is a grave factual error which demands, in the application of the standards of this Court, that this appeal Appeals Chamber substitutes these findings. The Prosecution itself admits that we cannot accept the testimony of witness Oklopcic. There were many errors in the conclusions here. We're talking about Witness Starcevic, for example. This is a witness brought by Mr. Fila, and in his testimony he decidedly said that he saw Kvocka in Omarska once and once only. The same witness, when he talked about his tasks when he came here, that he did have his posts to which he reported to, did he not have to report to anyone about his work. He knew what he was supposed to do. The Trial Chamber concluded that he was talking about Kvocka, that Kvocka did not have to report to anyone, that Kvocka did whatever he wanted and so on and so forth. I do not want to point to all of these errors, but just the fact that there is no consistency between the judgement and the indictment points to the conclusion of what the relationship of this had to have been to the conclusion. The conclusions were quite different. They came from things that were not mentioned by any witnesses. Not one single witness mentioned that Kvocka was deputy commander of the guards. Witness Alisic, mentioned by my learned colleagues yesterday, said that Kvocka said that he was camp commander. Which logical, legal, or any other kind of interpretations can lead to us draw the conclusion that this witness supported the fact that Kvocka was the equivalent of the deputy guards commander? This one-sided approach to the evidence was also viewed in the following: When my learned colleagues talk about the killing of Mulis [phoen] and Mehmedalija Nasic on the 20th of June don't mention Witness Okic Jasmir. Witness Okic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I take it Mr. Simic, you're about to conclude. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] My last sentence, Your Honour. Mr. Okic, an experienced policeman, a Bosniak himself, a direct eyewitness of the killing of the unfortunate Mehmedalija Nasic, watched the killing and he was questioned personally by the distinguished Judge Rodrigues with respect to the circumstances of the killing. And he said that Kvocka was not there. My learned colleagues did not mention that yesterday. All they did was mention one other witness and distorting his evidence. Thank you. Bearing in mind all these circumstances, we stand by our proposal that the remaining points in the indictment with respect to Kvocka should be rejected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Yes. Mr. Jovan Simic for Mr. Prcac. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Before I give my response, the Defence would like to repeat something that was said yesterday by the Prosecution or, rather, they tried to explain something to other people, that Zeljko Meakic was the commander of the camp. That is not true and correct. And in the judgement, paragraphs 29, 34, and 37, 39, the Trial Chamber concluded what the competencies of Zeljko Meakic were. In paragraph 372 they note that he was a leader of the security service in the Omarska camp. So the assertions made or, rather, the desires on the part of the Prosecution to have Zeljko Meakic be camp commander cannot stand and are unacceptable. The second point that I would like to raise at this point in time is that the Prosecution also claim that the system within the camp was illegal and unlawful and that people could withdraw and that he withdrew and that he was not punished. He mentioned DD10, Witness DD10, who left the camp and that nothing happened to him. From this allegedly the Trial Chamber concluded that anybody could leave the camp whenever they wanted to. DD10 was a witness who that worked in the Secret Service of the former Yugoslavia for a long time. DD10 was a witness who at the time of the war was also in the intelligence Secret Service, and DDD [as interpreted] was also a witness who said that he could leave the camp and nothing happened to them because the Secret Service of the former Yugoslavia stood behind him and that the service of Republika Srpska itself as well [as interpreted]. Your Honours, the indictment and Prosecution said yesterday that the -- that Mr. Prcac did not respond to the form of the indictment and that is true. The Defence team had no reason to object to the form of the indictment. You know that better than this Defence team itself, but it is one of the rare indictments which was confirmed before this Tribunal and which was precise in that way. Mr. Prcac, through the indictment, was accused of the counts we're all familiar with and charges we're all familiar with, but it also said that he was the deputy camp commander and responsible by virtue of that capacity and that he had certain authorisations such as that he was a superior to everyone there, that he had effective control, that he could have indeed changed the conditions in the camp, that he could say who was allowed to leave the camp and who was not, and that as deputy camp commander he was also responsible as a member of the joint criminal enterprise and, as we know, this responsibility is incorporated in Article 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Therefore, I think the Defence had a clear-cut position defined for Mr. Prcac. The acts that he allegedly perpetrated, the capacity he perpetrated them in, and some acts were concretised as well. The charges brought against him, which were to be proved as support to the indictment, which in the position of this Defence team was more than precise, and that is why we did not complain. We did not object to the indictment. So whatever the Prosecution claims, there was a precise indictment. The functions of the accused were set out. The authorisations were set out, et cetera, et cetera. The Prosecution did not wish to determine the form of joint criminal intent because I suppose they counted on the -- think that mens rea would be established through the trial and proceedings and that culpability would establish thereby. Perhaps they forgot, because the Prosecution teams replaced each other so many times they might have forgotten it. But what have they proved of the charges in the indictment? Nothing. Is there any identity there? No, there isn't, and the Prosecution confirmed that yesterday. The concept, the notion of concentration camp expounded by the Prosecution was mentioned for the first time, and we don't mind, towards the very end of the case itself, towards the end of the trial when there were no further possibilities of proving the first form of joint criminal intent. An administrative assistant to the camp commander as a concept was something the Defence heard the first time when the indictment was made -- when the judgement was made public, and the Defence wanted to say that the function is no longer important. What we have to see is what he actually did, what acts he actually committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, would you like to slow down a little. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, but I have very little time at my disposal, Your Honour. But I do apologise, yes. So the Prosecution yesterday tried to tell us that it didn't matter what actual function he held and that the Trial Chamber, that all of us here today had the role of establishing his function, his posts. Now I'm asking myself, and I'm asking all of us together, why then should a function be determined at all, a post be determined? Why was it -- the issue raised in the first place? Now, something that goes to the detriment of the Defence team, and I'm sure that the Appeals Chamber will find that in paragraph 468 point D, the Appeals Chamber says that Prcac's participation in the functioning of the camp as an administrative assistant to the camp commander was important, making him liable as a participant in the joint criminal enterprise of Omarska camp. That means, as I said on Wednesday, that I could agree if he was said to be a member of the joint criminal enterprise, if that's what the Prosecution said, and then the Defence team would be duty-bound to look into all the possibilities of his having taken part in a joint criminal enterprise. But with a precisely defined indictment of this kind and the conclusion made by the Court in the paragraph that I just quoted, there is absolutely no dilemma that the identity is wrong between the indictment and the judgement and that this is to the detriment of the Defence team because they never actually discussed the matter. The Defence team would like to present one further point. If in keeping with continental law, perhaps, the Trial Chamber wished to ascertain the truth as it stood, the material truth as it is called in continental law, it was duty-bound either to instruct the Prosecution to amend the indictment because the Prosecution says that is just one part of the case. Yes, that is why can and should be amended [as interpreted], if the situation during trial is different from what has been set out or if the conditions are ripe for that. So what it should have done is this: It should have either instructed the Prosecution to amend the indictment and now to prove the assertions which emanate from the factual -- from the facts or, as in the Stakic case, it could call witnesses to establish who the commander was, whether there was an administrative assistant, what his authority was, did he have an important contribution, et cetera, et cetera, or whether they were important matters for that particular camp or the application of a joint criminal enterprise liability generally. In its appeal -- appellant's brief, the Defence also stated, although the Prosecution yesterday did try to relativise this, if I can put it that way, that Mr. Prcac did not take part in any individual crime in paragraphs 451 and 458, and the Trial Chamber concluded that. Now, what the Defence wants to point out to this Appeals Chamber is the following fact: That the conclusion made by the Trial Chamber itself, that Mr. Prcac was an administrative assistant is erroneous. We don't have time to go into this, whether he came of his own free will or not, volitionally or not, but the Trial Chamber did conclude that he never mentioned it himself in an interview to the Prosecution and that written documents state otherwise. Speculations on the subject of whether the witness can recognise and identify somebody or cannot once again is stated in the indictment that there were at least two of them, two perpetrators and that one of them could have been Prcac. No 10 or 15 witnesses were called on that day to recognise and identify the people. Now, the insinuations made by the Prosecution that Mr. Prcac called out 20 and as they weren't on the list they were listed as missing, we can see in the list that they are alive and well and were transferred to Manjaca camp. The other assertion that the Defence said that he was the administrative assistant, let me address that now. Although I don't have time to do that, I will just quote the following: The Court said that he was in charge of the transfer of detainees and that is found in footnote 702. He list -- he read out lists of persons being transferred and that the -- that the Defence brought this up in its pre-trial brief. The Defence wrote that he read out lists of persons who were transferred to Trnopolje and Manjaca. That was the transfer of women. They all reached those camps alive and well, and all of them also turned up alive and well. Now, had the Defence actually wrote this, it could have drawn a conclusion, but erroneously quoting a conclusion of this kind on the pre-trial -- the Defence brief led to the erroneous conclusion on the part of the Trial Chamber. I should now like to look through the lists, and read through the lists, and Mr. Prcac's authority in compiling these lists and his responsibility. Yesterday the Prosecution, once again, for the umpteenth time, and it has done this consistently from the beginning of trial, once again stated that Mr. Prcac was in charge of the lists, that he compiled the lists, and these were not ordinary lists. They were lists after which people were tortured, disappeared, et cetera, et cetera, beaten and so on, and that that was his administrative duty in compiling those lists. Well, that is just not true, just not correct, Your Honour, because there is no evidence and proof of that in this case. Perhaps there are in some other trials but not in this particular case. Now, as far as the administrative duties are concerned of Mr. Prcac I would like to state following: None of the witnesses explained what those duties were. All they said was he carried papers around. In the former Yugoslavia, yes, when people carried documents we would say he was a clerk or whatever, depending on the language and terms you're used to. But nobody said that he kept records, compiled lists, et cetera, and the Defence says this with full responsibility. He never did that. Point number 2: Apart from having said that he carried papers and lists around, none of the witnesses quoted a single name, the name of a person read out from a particular list, read out by Mr. Prcac, and that as a result that individual disappeared. All they said was they read that -- that he read the list, but they said that -- and here we'll come to the famous sentence that they were tortured or disappeared answer. Then my cross-examination was, I asked them to give me one name. They couldn't name a single name. The same witness gave 25 non-Serb names of people who were beaten or disappeared in some other way. Now, with respect to compiling the lists, we raised this matter on Wednesday. The lists were compiled by the interrogators. They were compiled at the public security station in Prijedor, and nobody compiled the lists in Omarska camp itself either amongst the Security Service led by Zeljko Meakic. There is no proof or evidence of that at all. So anybody to draw that conclusion, and I do apologise because Mr. Fila mentioned this standard a moment ago, but that person cannot make a -- that is not a reasonable person to make such a conclusion. There is no proof or evidence of that. And what has troubled the Defence team from the general -- from the very beginning is the constant pressure on behalf of the Prosecution to create an atmosphere conducive to Mr. Prcac's participation in all this and that he was in charge of compiling these lists. There is absolutely no proof of evidence of that, and I'm sure that the Appeals Chamber will become convinced of that in due course. May I summarise. The administrative assistant to the camp commander is a function that determine Mr. Prcac's position in the joint criminal enterprise, and it determined that he is criminally responsible pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute. Let me just briefly add the following and tell you why we feel aggrieved. The Defence thanked the Trial Chamber at the end. They had a lot of understanding for us. We were given just one and a half months to prepare our Defence. However, this Defence team did not express its gratitude to the Prosecution. I was not able to thank the Prosecution for a bona fide relationship towards us because we were tripped up many times and were not disclosed the material we should have been disclosed. Witness K, for example, in talking to the Prosecution said that she would mention Prcac, although she never mentioned Prcac up until then. The Prosecution did not inform us of that. When the Defence asked that that portion of the transcript be redacted, they said this came out spontaneously. We ascertained that it was not spontaneous, but never mind, we left that alone. Witness Nihad Haskic was introduced with the explanation that he would be a specific witness with respect to his testimony of Mr. Prcac, and another nine witnesses but Mr. Haskic never mentioned him in his testimony. Other material that was not disclosed to us also exists. I'm sorry, but I cannot -- now that I don't have time to elaborate on all this undisclosed material. There are many things that speak about mens rea with respect to our accused to what was going on. I haven't got the time to address all that but in any case, the Defence had a very poor relationship, unfortunately, with the Prosecution, not this team but the other Prosecution team. And finally the closing arguments of our Defence team were geared towards not refuting certain allegations but erroneous quotations by the Prosecution in their own closing statement. So these are problems which made our task much more difficult with the short time span that we had at our disposal, and at this point in time the Defence feels that this resulted in the fact that a completely precise indictment burst like a bubble, and we had to save what we could because the Trial Chamber did quote erroneously and accorded itself the right of stepping outside the identity and frameworks of the indictment and take on the role of Prosecutor itself. Your Honours, with respect to Mr. Prcac himself and his own relationship. He has given an interview, and in his interview he set out the elements he thought to be the vital essential elements. It was the fault of the Prosecution that they did not investigate the details, and then they cannot ascribe that to us. If they -- if somebody says there were two corpses there, why don't they be -- why aren't they taken away, it is not because they didn't matter. There was the proposal of hearing Mr. Prcac himself as a witness, but due to his health we did not call Mr. Prcac as a witness in the end. And finally, Mr. Prcac is what he is. We provided enough details. The Defence has already mentioned that some things simply could not have been done differently. Mr. Prcac could not have not gone to the camp. He was there under duress. He was forced to be there and simply that forced -- the reason why he was there under duress was to save his family. He had two sons. He has two sons who are handicapped. The non-activity of Mr. Prcac, because as I said there is no evidence that he was involved in any crimes or committed anything directly was actually what he did was to save himself. He believed that if he had to be there, at least if he did nothing, that would make his position a bit easier. He felt that if he stayed there but did nothing, he would spare himself. Finally, Your Honours, mistakes are possible. We are all liable to commit mistakes, and it's important also to admit that if that happens. I hope that this Defence has convinced the Appeals Chamber of their submissions and that the Appeals Chamber will correct the injustice perpetrated on Mr. Prcac and that it will reach a decision to acquit. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I explain to you that I've since been educated, and I realised that what happened was that there was no deliberate act of discrimination where your client is concerned. What was done was, regard was had to the size of the cases, and that's why you were given 15 minutes, which time period was related to the fact that you were given one hour to begin with. Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not even think that. I was just joking. So please take that as a joke. It was not meant to be a serious comment. I will respond very briefly to the submissions of the Prosecution. The Prosecution claims that 65 ter was done after the disclosure of the material so that they were not obliged to act in accordance with Rule 65 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I think that they were right, because the trial was still under way, and rules are applied to any proceedings that are under way. For an additional argument, it's true that during the trial proceedings rules were changed in relation to the use of affidavits, and the Trial Chamber then decided that nevertheless, in the interests of justice they will continue to use affidavits even though this was now not allowed under the Rules. Had the Trial Chamber decided not to apply 65 ter, then they could have decided in the interests of justice not to apply that rule, but as they did not reach such a decision, 65 ter bound or obliged both the Defence and the Prosecution. The same thing applies for Rule 63 of the Rules which says that the -- that 63, and I have just quoted from that, at no moment did the Prosecution say in relation to Witness AT say that she was being questioned in relation to Rule 93(A). So for the first time we found out about this from the judgement and not from the Prosecution. The Prosecution also claims that I was not right to ask to -- for it to have established any reasonable doubt that the testimony of Witness T [as interpreted] was true, because they say this was not taken as testimony in the sense of facts but only as to conduct. At that moment, the ad contrario argument led to the conclusion that it was not important whether Witness T was speaking the truth or not when we are using this as an example of conduct. Yes. I apologise once again. I will write this down for myself. I'm speaking too fast. So we cannot accept such a standard, because if you are using testimony by a witness as evidence of a pattern of conduct, then this testimony has to be true and subject to the tests of any other testimony. So the testimony of Witness T -- AT has to be as true as the testimony of any other witness on which the judgement is based. And now I'm talking -- I'm finished dealing with 65 ter and 93. As far as Witness F, Sifeta Susic, and Zlata Cikota, I almost foresaw that Judge Weinberg de Roca would ask that question, and I wrote down the sentence for myself which the Prosecution does not seem to understand. The Defence claims that rape in itself as a rape and sexual assault undoubtedly are grave violations of international humanitarian law. This is clear. But as the Defence disputes the value of the use of the testimony of K and AT, the Defence claims that without K and this T [as interpreted], just these three statements would not amount to serious violations in the sense of Article 2. So this is what I'm claiming. I'm not saying it's clear that I'm right. I'm just saying that it's very clear what my submission is. We need to keep in mind, though, that when we're talking about Witness J, there are misunderstandings between myself and the Prosecution because as I said, in the judgement as far as Witness J is concerned, the Trial Chamber found that this was an attempted rape. So this is a little bit more than what refers to Witness F, Susic, and Cikota. The Prosecution claims that this is not so, but I'm asking the Appeals Chamber to read paragraph 574 of the judgement, and there you will see Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. clearly what we are talking about. I'm not clear either about yesterday's discussion about 7(3), because if I understand the Prosecution correctly, it would seem that it is not correct that Radic was acquitted of 7(3) but that the Trial Chamber had made no judgement on that. To the contrary. It is clear that the Trial Chamber did not discuss 7(3) because they found that there was no reason to do that. So why would they deliberate on something that wasn't there? This is how I understood it. As far as another very important question, this is something new on which my colleague dwelt to some extent yesterday, and this is the question of Witness K once again. As you know, I said several times that Mr. Radic denies any contact with any of the witnesses. I never said that he had any kind of contact on a voluntary basis so that then I would have an explanation about the national jurisdictions and so on. I don't know where that comes from. I know it's been discussed in the Prosecution, but I don't know how that applies here. What the Defence actually said was that it was incorrect to present the Kunarac judgement after the appeal, which was made after the appeal, and why I did not look at the Kunarac appeal judgement, because I was not able to do that because at the time that had not been finished yet. I also could not use the arguments -- just one moment. I need to find it. Yes. As far as the Sikirica case is concerned and the judgement in that case, the Prosecution says why didn't I make a submission in the sense of 94(B) to have this accepted as a fact in respect to that Rule. The reason is simple. The Omarska -- the Omarska case was completed before the judgement was made. So I could not deal with that retroactively. Therefore, in the sense of 94(B), I could not ask for the acceptance of an adjudicated facts from the Keraterm case because at the time this was not done. I am pointing out that this is important, that two Trial Chambers in relation to the same witness and the same facts, rape, came to two different positions just like as in the case of Witness J. I forgot to mention this. I forgot to mention this captain, that she gives the same description which refer to two persons. So I don't know whether this was a mixing up of two people or it's a false statement. So this is my example. For example, as you say, Zeljko Marmat and some Karate Kid, but they are actually one in the same person and in this case they are being described as two people. So we don't need to go further into that. So we could not ask for judicial notice of adjudicated facts in the sense of Rule 94, but we are being asked to consider as new facts which had already damaged the credibility of Witness K, and this was established already by the Trial Chamber in their judgement. And the judgement was made based on proposals by the Prosecution who themselves did not believe Witness K, that she had been raped by Sikirica, even though she claimed that the entire time. This is a very unreliable witness, and I repeat, had the Prosecution decided -- managed to prove their case based on the testimony of Witness A, there would have been no need for Witness K to appear and testify at all. Just one minor detail relating to the shifts. The Trial Chamber never dealt with the fact that anybody ever worked outside of their shift in the camp, and none of the witnesses confirmed anything like that, and this is why the position of Hase Icic's position was disputed because he had seen him in the morning and in the evening, be this is simply not possible. And finally, allow me to conclude. We may a considerable objection to the indictment, and this was also discussed by the other -- my learned friends regarding the joint criminal enterprise. I believe that we are actually talking about something else here. At the point in time when the indictment was drafted, and as you know this is one of the first indictments, this Court did not deal so much with the criminal enterprise. This does not mean that this was not known in international law, it's just that this court did not deal with that to such an extent. And I believe that due to the change-over of the Prosecution teams, they decided to prove the indictment by confidential schedules and through the events, and when they saw that the indictment would not be able to stand up to that and that the indictment was not proved, the Trial Chamber saved the indictment from being completely dismissed by using this joint criminal enterprise. So the trial now is saving the indictment because there was no identity between the indictment and the judgement. I agree that nobody should be a blinkered horse, as was mentioned by my learned friend from the Prosecution. I said that in continental law we stick to the indictment like a horse with blinkers, who does not look to the left or to the right. It sees nothing more than the indictment. So if I am behaving like a blinkered Defence counsel, I do not accept the claim that I am a blind Defence counsel. So I would like to have these charges dismissed, especially the charges relating to the rapes, because I do not agree that this is something that Radic is proving his joint criminal intent through. I'm claiming that there is no rape. I believe that the judgement should be dismissed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. May I propose --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- or accepted in the terms that I have put forth. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, may I propose -- I see on the schedule that we've issued we're not supposed to take a break until 11.25. But may I suggest that we take a break and return after the break to hear Mr. Zigic through his counsel Mr. Stojanovic, and then the parties themselves. Is that agreeable? Then we shall suspend for 30 minutes in the usual way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now the sitting is resumed. We give the floor to counsel for Mr. Zigic, I think. Yes. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Perhaps I'll start in the reverse order and respond to some questions raised by Your Honours yesterday. The Defence of the accused Zigic availed itself of its right to cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses. Every witness who mentioned Zigic in whatever context was cross-examined by the Defence team, and even those who did not mention him, too, but whose testimony could have had something to do with Zigic's indictment. We cross-examined Mrkalj Edin whose testimony says that in describing the events that took place on the same day that Becir Medunjanin was killed with the instrument that Becir Medunjanin was killed with in Omarska, that Zoran Vokic beat him up, and that is, on the transcript, 2931. So that is the line. So not Zoran Zigic. The man who was mentioned was Zoran Vokic. And he was described as Fadil Avdagic describes the killer of Becir Medunjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What is true is that when we questioned all the witnesses or during the trial itself, we never said we didn't believe them or that they were lying. But the wrong conclusion has been deduced from this, namely we are thought to have claimed that we agreed to what they said by doing so. Now a few words about joint criminal enterprise. This is something that my learned colleague Ms. Rashid spoke at length about, but so did the other members of the Prosecution team as well. Although this Defence team speaks about the problems of a category of this kind in principle, it objects to this broad understanding of the concept of joint criminal enterprise which incorporates Zigic into it as well. Zigic is here as an outsider. He is mentioned in various ways in that way compared to the other accused. It would appear that neither my colleague Re has understood us properly. So let us repeat what we said. The judgement, as indeed the indictment, portrays joint criminal enterprise not as a mode of viability but as a specific crime, and that crime is called the Omarska camp, whereas it is not provide for by the Tribunal's Statute. We're not going to repeat all that argumentation now because we've already put it forward in our appellant's brief. But be that as it may, if the indictment and judgement said it was a mode of liability, let that stand. But tell us now, please, what, what part? I haven't learnt that to this day. Or, rather, to make matters simple, let's take the mode of liability expressed in assistance. We're going to say that the Prosecution informed us that Zigic assisted without informing whether he assisted or aided and abetted in persecution, torture, inhumane acts or anything else. Judging by paragraph 691 of the judgement, Zigic was found guilty not only for persecution through joint criminal enterprise but also for killings within the joint criminal enterprise, and this can be seen from the way in which the killings in Omarska were formulated, and torture within joint criminal enterprise. All the tortures in Omarska, but also each of these things individually and separately. The judgement quoted several instances of joint criminal enterprise in -- by courts and tribunals after the war, but we didn't hear an example quoted that could be compared to the Zigic case, that is to say, somebody who spent just half an hour in a camp and who in no way took part in the establishment of the camp, in supplying the camp, maintaining it, or anything like that. He was never employed there. He never occupied any position there. If they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Just on a point of order, and out of an abundance of caution, it is my understanding that Witness A testified in closed session so that in fact we may have to redact and possibly go into private session if my friend in fact intends to bring up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if that is correct and you desire to proceed, then would it be convenient if we went into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I have completed what I wanted to say. I don't think I disclosed anything that is confidential, but of course if that passage should be redacted, I agree to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. We will redact that passage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: If I may, it's at the beginning of his submissions, yes.
