utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they had only related the Essen lynch case or Borkum Island that we referred to, I have to say that I always had a great deal of difficulty in understanding what is sometimes called implicit criminal responsibility and liability. I think that that term should not be used at all. I am of the opinion that in situations of this kind, it is far better to use a more precise, just, and simple theory of co-perpetration as was applied to the Stakic case. Quite obviously under the German school and Professor Claus Roxin with a great deal of assistance from Judge Schomburg. After that trial I went to have lunch in the canteen, but I don't know why, whether because I was hungry or to further the work of the canteen itself. As I eat a lot, I will certainly promote business in the canteen. Now, this latter possibility never occurred to me before. However, it is not a criminal activity, so let me use another example to illustrate to what I want to say. As the registry is not paying me, I'm going to rob a bank, and there I'm going to link myself up with some local criminals. Let's take that example. I know that in that way, I will considerably further crime in this city. I'll probably set an example to some so that they could copy me or do something similar. Now, if I'm caught, I don't suppose they're going to accuse me of being responsible for all the crimes taking part in this city even before or afterwards, or even while I'm in Belgrade. Finally, in putting off a final assertion with respect to Becir Medunjanin's murder and the torture of Witness D for later as the most important charges brought against Zigic in Omarska, the Prosecution will also have to put a discussion on his participation in the joint criminal enterprise in Omarska. Now something about my "frivolous" brief, mentioned by my dear colleague Carmona, and there is a misunderstanding on that score too. The Prosecution received instructions from the Trial Chamber that all confidential documents should be made public and that protected witnesses should just be given a pseudonym and confidentiality respected in that light. And this happened to the Judge and to acquittal [as interpreted] when several charges in the indictment were struck. The Prosecution after that makes the same contribution as it did twice before. One was a completely confidential document and contains all the charges, whereas the other one was completely public and open. And in the submissions, all the incidents that were rejected pursuant to Rule 98 bis were rejected. They were brought up again. The pre-appeals Judge was asked what that meant. I asked him, "What does this mean?" And this is topical today. What does the Prosecution's position mean, that the torture of Abdulah Brkic was both public and confidential? The answer I was given was that I was frivolous, and in my appeal, paragraph 269 in my appeals brief, I wrote that after that I came to realise that in the indictment and the charges this indeed did not mean anything but that it was necessary for the Prosecution to inform us in advance what has no sense in the indictment and the charges so that we're not confused by this. And I'm still not clear on that today. How can a single fact at one and the same time be both public and confidential? And that the person should be charged again for charges that were rejected previously. Now with respect to Mr. Re's presentation, and he refers to the Kupreskic case and the appellant's brief in that case. I should like to say that it would be a good idea if all the standards from that judgement were applied to this case too. And we set that out in our appeals brief, especially those which refer to the identification of the perpetrators. We all know what happened. However, in paragraph 158 of our appellant's brief, we also refer to the following passage, and I'm now going to read out that passage to you. It says: "In any case, the Appeals Chamber in the Kupreskic case, [in English] Kupreskic Appeals Chamber judgement, paragraph 39 upheld the opinion stated by the Canadian Court of Appeal in Regina versus Harper. Where the report including the Reasons for Judgement discloses a lack of appreciation of relevant evidence and more particularly the complete disregard of such evidence, then it falls upon the reviewing Tribunal to intercede. This standpoint refers to Zigic's case as a whole as previously elaborated and not only with respect to the murder of Emsud Bahonjic." [Interpretation] The assertion of the Prosecution in this portion, that is to say that they didn't see where justice had been impinged upon, does not stand. I think that the Prosecution must respect the fact that the appellant comes to the Appeals Chamber not as to some people who have to be explain the most elemental and basic -- elementary and basic things, but with all due respect to their vast knowledge and experience, they are presenting their own case, their appellant's brief, of course in summary form, which will give them enough time for their own deliberations and decision-making. Now, is it up to us to explain to the Trial Chamber something which is the A, B, C of law, the basic facts of law? We could expect quite the reverse, in actual fact. The response by the other side with respect to persecution it seems to be that I am prone to certain political, raising certain political arguments. I would like to define policy and politics according to Hans Kelsen's premise, but not to -- I'm not going to mention that here and now. The Prosecution does not provide an answer to this position's defence about political persecution. It seems to be adhering to the dogma on persecution as exists in the Tribunal's practice so far, which, as we can see from the general principles of the work of the Tribunal, is subject to further criticism and new approaches. With regard to Zigic's regular access to Omarska, the Prosecution relies on the testimony by Azedin Oklopcic, and he is the witness of Becir Medunjanin's killing who was quite categoric in saying that Zigic did not take part in that act. He said that categorically, and he gave us the names of the people who took part in it, although he doesn't wish Zigic well at all and doesn't have a good opinion of Zigic himself. Now, what are we going to believe? Are we going to believe the Prosecution or Oklopcic? Now, the Prosecution and the judgement gives an unacceptable recipe there of all the witnesses we have to squeeze out of them those things that are in favour of the indictment even if it goes one or two drops in favour of the accused and reject anything else without giving any explanations for doing so. The witness himself spoke untruths with respect to Zigic. He said that Zigic had beaten up Beganovic which was refuted by the judgement because Beganovic himself said he did not beat him up. What is lacking here is a comment on the testimonies made by over 60 witnesses who were in Omarska and who claimed they never saw Zigic in Omarska or that they saw him only once. A couple of them, whether they were victims or alleged victims, say precisely that, including Witness T, Witness AK, Witness AJ, and Abdulah Brkic himself. As has already been said, the Prosecution will state its final position with regard to the killing of Becir Medunjanin in due course but it nonetheless contests the allegations of the appellant. The appellant would like to draw the Chambers attention to something that is shocking. Zigic way back in 1998 was accused of the killing of Becir Medunjanin. However, the whole and most competent and complex team of Prosecutors, Grant Niemann, Michael Keegan, and Kapila Waidyaratne and Dan Saxon, being members of that team, signed a document submission pursuant to Rule 73 bis (B)(ii), and filed it with the court on the 17th of September, 1999 in which on page 49 of the B/C/S text they say that they do not see how Zigic can be accused of the killing of Medunjanin without a single scrap of evidence or proof, and that that should be placed within the general counts in the indictment. Therefore, that is a statement made by the top men in the Prosecution, and it is part of the documents that have been filed. I should like to draw the Appeals Chamber's attention to it, a statement given after the indictment was raised. And so we ask ourselves on the basis of which an indictment was raised at all against Zigic in that respect. Regarding the conviction for the killing of Bahonjic, we repeat there was no deliberation. There are no proofs that anything stated by the Defence was reviewed at all. Then what can be done in the appeal according to the proposal by the Prosecution, since this is not a de novo proceedings? It remains for the entire Defence, with over 1.000 pages of witness statements and three expert witnesses' reports, should be rejected which was all submitted to the Trial Chamber which in turn ignored all of that. We must stress that we provided many arguments against a conviction which were individually sufficient to be successful and that the Prosecutor yesterday responded to only one of those submissions. The Prosecution in its response says the Defence talks about a game of numbers from which it is evident they did not carefully read our appeal, our brief and that they provided arguments -- where we provided arguments that this in fact was not a matter of significance. In the killing of Drago Tokmadzic, in the view of the Defence there are about ten reasons, each one of which is individually responsible for an acquittal, and we believe that the response of the Prosecution does not deal with the basis of any of our claims. As far as Brkic's claims, who is not favourable toward Zigic, he said that Zigic -- I stress, Zigic never harmed him in any way and that, again, he never beat him. So the stress is on never, which is repeated twice, but there is also the absence of other proof that Zigic tortured Brkic. And when the Prosecution and even more the judgement bases so much of their decisions on this witness, why is there no explanation provided that they believe him in all of the charges against Zigic but do not believe anything he says which goes to the benefit of Zigic; for example, in the killing of Medunjanin and the torture of Witness T. As far as the beating of Witness AK, which Zigic admitted, and we're only dealing now with the fact why he did that from which we need to draw a precise qualification of this criminal act. Witness AK did not give an answer to this, and Zigic said this was done for certain personal reasons. This is not sufficient proof that he only did that because he was a Muslim. So we're only talking about a qualification for admission of a crime. I'm also at the end, but I think that this is a good moment to comment on today's submissions by our colleague which talked about the sentencing. On page 12 of today's transcript, she said that Zigic took money from AK. I really don't know why my colleague did that. This is absolutely untrue. Zigic is charged with a lot already in the indictment and by the judgement, so then there is no need to add more things on top of that without any grounds about any witness statements or any other piece of evidence. There is no evidence that he took any money from AK, as my learned colleague claimed today. In connection with certain convictions based on the statement of only one witness, the Prosecution refers to a certain practice of the Tribunal which says that this can be done. This was done, but there were other factors present and as an exception, but the rule is that exceptions should be interpreted very closely. However, this practice in that context says that the Trial Chamber can do this but that it is not obliged to do so. All in all, the Prosecution comes to the conclusion based on this that the statement of one sole witness is always enough and treats this as a rule and not as an exception. And what is worse, we're not talking about one statement, but one statement which is contradicted by four other statements which don't need to be mentioned at all. So according to the Prosecution, the rule is that one witness is sufficient even though his evidence is contrary to the testimony of ten other witnesses, but here we have the question, which other witnesses? Why only those who are favourable to their case? By constantly referring to exceptions, we will come to a situation where we will create a backward-looking rule. Regarding the statement of Hasan Karabasic, we must remain by our position that triviality is a term used by the Prosecution in respect of this incident. I must say that Prosecution witnesses also said that Zigic was very careful in watching over Karabasic while Karabasic was in Keraterm. This was stated by Safet Taci. Another witness, a witness of the Defence does not dispute a certain conflict but he claims that on that occasion Zigic came to Trnopolje to bring a food package to a friend of his, a Muslim, and finally again another Prosecution witness who stated that Zigic strangled him with one hand only because his other hand was hurt, which does not fit into the testimonies of other witnesses. And finally just a few remarks about the Prosecution's submissions today. My learned colleague said that Zigic had 13 cases of beatings, and in paragraph 691(C) we counted nine such incidents, plus one gross mishandling in item 9.D. We stated four different arguments in our appeal brief. We actually stated many arguments, but because of the time restraints we only referred to four of them in our oral submissions. As far as Banovic is concerned, I think that in spite of a detailed explanation by my learned friend, nobody in the world would understand this. Banovic, five killings; Zigic, four. Banovic, 27 beatings; Zigic, nine. As far as the circumstances are concerned, I've already said before that Banovic is faced with many more unfavourable circumstances than Zigic is. We believe that this ratio is not good when we are considering the authority of this Tribunal. And finally, based on the submissions of the Prosecution, perhaps I misunderstood, but it seems to me that the message that can be drawn is followed. Do not admit anything. Do not express your remorse. Do not show any goodwill towards the Tribunal. We're thinking about Zigic's surrender here. And you can only do this only if it is all in accordance with the positions of the Prosecution. This is something that we cannot agree with. I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. I would be interested in knowing the reaction of Ms. Howick to your statement that she alleged that Zigic had taken money from Witness K when there was no evidence of that. Ms. Howick, would you answer very briefly what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOWICK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I either misspoke or if it was translated differently, I meant to say demanded money. I did not mean to say took. And if that is how it -- I either said it I was mistaken, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay, I understand you. Well, then -- Yes, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I recall correctly the transcript, he did not demand the money but he said that this was due to some earlier conflicts that they had before in relation to procuring fuel and petrol, something to this effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We have been forewarned, and we will look up the transcript ourselves. Thank you. Mr. Carmona, you are on your legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed. I just wish to crave the indulgence of this learned Tribunal in addressing a concern, particularly in relation to the nature of reply. My learned friend on the other side has referred to some document that was filed by the Prosecution on the 17th of September, 1999. This is not in any substantive brief, neither is it in our arguments, and I think out of an abundance of caution and fairness the Prosecution will reserve a right to respond, if not at the evidentiary hearing that is in fact coming sometime in the future, or if not, certainly in fact by the appropriate filed document. We just wish to reserve that right at this point in time. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We don't think that -- you're not insisting on that are you, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may make a correction. We're talking about Witness AK and not Witness A. About the matters discussed, my learned friend Mr. Carmona, I am asking in the final trial brief or in the appellant's brief of argument. I'm looking for it but this is something that is stated in our written documents, and I'm looking for the place right now. I hope that I will be able to find it. This is the place where we refer to that particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Carmona, Mr. Stojanovic says that he was speaking of another witness, and perhaps you might not wish to pursue the matter then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: I'm just out of an abundance of caution, given the fact that he spoke about some kind of document filed by the Prosecutors in relation to the alleged killing of Becir Medunjanin, I just thought that out of an abundance of caution I would need to examine in fact this and find out what is the state of affairs in relation to this particular document and, if need be, respond accordingly. If it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, in that case, Mr. Stojanovic will have a right of reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just found it. It's paragraph 141, our appellant's brief of argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Paragraph 141. May I suggest we have reached a stage where we ought to be moving forward now, and so we have come to the point where the appellants personally have a right to address the Court individually, and I would suggest seven minutes each. So I would now call on Mr. Kvocka. THE APPELLANT KVOCKA: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at the end of these long trial proceedings, all that remains for me is a faith in justice. I have been charged as a commander of a camp and also deputy commander of the camp, and the news on my indictment, arrest, and trial has been covered by world media. I have been acquitted of these serious charges, but the newspapers and the media, even in my country, still today write or say, "Kvocka, former commander of the Omarska camp." This is something that can no longer be stopped or changed. I have almost served my sentence. Your Honours, I have children. I have grandchildren. And over these past few days in this courtroom, I am seeking justice so that from that they can be freed of accusations that their father and grandfather was a criminal. I can say that I have not violated God's or man's laws, and I'm so sure of that that I am quite able to say that God can repay me all the evil that I allegedly committed or wished on anyone in that Omarska camp. I am aware of the suffering and the pain of many people in the war. I feel very sorry for the people who were in Omarska and in Celebici and Dretelj and feel sorry for the pain of any people anywhere who suffered. But, Your Honours, my conscience is clear. I did not intentionally or unintentionally harm anyone; quite to the contrary. I helped as much as I could. And please believe me, the times were very difficult. I am just asking this Honourable Tribunal to deliberate on all the submissions made by my lawyer over the past few days, and justice is my last hope. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kvocka. May we hear from Mr. Radic. THE APPELLANT RADIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I been have charged before this Tribunal for command responsibility and for the specific crime of rape of Witness A. In the first instance judgement of this Tribunal of the Trial Chamber, I was acquitted of the command responsibility charges and acquitted of charges for rape of Witness A so that my indictment was overturned and I am a free man. From that moment on until this very day, we have just been dealing with impossibilities and improbabilities. Your Honours, I do not understand the intricacies of legal matters, and I will not say anything that has not already been said before this Tribunal, but I still would like to claim for myself the right to say a couple of things. First of all as a person, I would like to express my sympathy with the sufferings of all the victims in that region no matter whether they belong to the Muslim, Croat, or ethnic national group or any other group. I really sympathise with all of those victims. Gentlemen, I have imprisoned for exactly 2.180 days, or, to be exact, 12 more days will make a full six years or 2.193 days. This is my fate and I cannot change it. But as a man I am hurt about the things I have learned in this courtroom and in our case, as well as the things I have read in the media about what kind of things certain individuals committed, which crimes and ill deeds they committed, and based on plea agreements to learn what kind of sentences they were given. I will not discuss any plea agreement or plea bargain, but I have to ask myself here, why have I been imprisoned for so long, for many years and my proceedings have still not yet been finished nor any of the charges against me have been proved. As the third and most important thing I would like to say so that the whole world can hear me, whoever on this planet wants war - no matter where they happen to be or no matter to which people or nation they belong to and no matter what the colour of their skin - whoever wants war, I hope they have this war in their own home and feel it on their own skin, and I hope that war is not repeated any time, anywhere, because we all know that war does in the bring any good to anybody but only death, destruction, and misery. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Radic. Mr. Prcac. THE APPELLANT PRCAC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was arrested on the 5th of March, 2000. The trial began on the 2nd of May, 2000. The time for preparation of my trial was about two months. Before that I was retired. I was a pensioner and have been since 1995. During the war conflicts I was mobilised. Under threats and pressure I was made to work in the Omarska Investigation Centre regardless of my own will. I told that to the investigators of the OTP. I explained how I came to work in the Investigation Centre. On the 13th of March, 2000, I pled before this -- before the Trial Chamber as I am pleading now. I am not guilty of the charges brought against me in the indictment. Let me remind you that in judicial systems an indictment can be rejected if there is not sufficient evidence to bear it out. Your Honours, Judges, you were not able to ascertain or establish that I committed any crime at all, nor did I have any command responsibility. And on those grounds you were to establish my innocence and not to assume my guilt, and on the basis of assuming my guilt to pronounce sentence against me. This Court must compensate for the victims of the crimes that were perpetrated, but it also has to protect me if I'm innocent. My participation in the preparation or perpetration of criminal acts does not exist. Therefore, I consider myself to be innocent. In the fourth amended indictment, the Prosecutor states that at one point in time, I was the deputy commander of the investigations centre, which is not true, and that is why the Trial Chamber established that that was not proved, that it was not proved that I was in actual fact the deputy commander but that I was the administrative assistant of the centre in Omarska. The Trial Chamber also established that I had certain influence in Omarska and that I wielded some sort of power in the centre. Can you tell me what influence I wielded in Omarska? As an administrative assistant, I was a pensioner doing these jobs provisionally. What power did I have in the investigating centre? I was just a pensioner, a retired person. I had no power. I wasn't an administrative assistant anywhere. All I was was a clerk. If you have the name of the commander -- I'm sure you will have the name of a commander who will be able to tell you whether I was assistant administrative worker or not. I was charged under Article 7(1) for some material facts with respect to my participation in a joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecutor said I had significant contribution in that enterprise via the post and functions I performed in the Omarska camp. The Prosecutor says Prcac must have been informed of the nature of his authority in the investigations centre of Omarska. What functions can an administrative assistant have, even if he does exist? He is a -- if he is a pensioner, if he is retired? The Trial Chamber says that Prcac had certain control on the movement of detainees within the Investigation Centre and outside it. This is not true because in performing my duties and tasks, I never performed that one. The Trial Chamber also accepted on the basis of the testimony of just one Prosecution witness, (redacted) , who said that the guards would refer to me if they had a problem. Now this testimony of this witness is not truthful. We know to whom the guards were subordinated and to whom they applied for guidance. They did not do so -- come to me. I never -- I was never in charge of the transfer of detainees from one camp to another or one place to another. That did not come within the realm of my competence. The respondent on page 225 says that the Trial Chamber, furthermore, in paragraphs 452 noticed that Witness A was a protected witness and in the transcript - this is on 5487 and 564 - says that Witness F was a protected witness. This is also expressed in line 538 where he says that Prcac took female detainees out. I can say here and now that I never called out any female witnesses, and this was confirmed by (redacted) when asked by the president of the Trial Chamber, Judge Almiro Rodrigues, whether lady detainees were taken out at night. She said no, women were not called out at night. And you can refer to the transcript of that testimony. And these assertions are contrary to what Prosecution witnesses stated. A protected witness, Witness A said that I called out Zlata Cikota and that when she returned she was crying and quiet. I never called out Zlata Cikota during the night or any other women. So that is not a truthful statement by this witness. Zlata Cikota in this courtroom testified herself in this case. She testified against me and other individuals. Now, the statement she made is not true because Zlata Cikota would have said it first of all, when she first testified. This testifies to the kind of Prosecution witness she is. Zlata Cikota during her testimony said that I saved her life, and the Trial Chamber established that the position of Prcac was so insignificant as not to be termed that he took part in a joint criminal enterprise. That speaks to my work at the investigative centre. I had 11 hour shifts, 12-hour shirts and nothing more than that. All I did was working on radio and communication devices and telephone communication. Your Honours, I would like to remind you that during the presentation of Prosecution evidence, several witnesses testified, five of which did not identify and recognise me in this courtroom. Seventeen Prosecution witnesses didn't know what kind of work I did at all, what tasks I performed, and that is sufficient testimony to what all this is about. There were many contradictory witness testimonies, secondhand hearsay evidence was presented. My health has been ruined. I have been punished by -- I was punished by SFOR before my guilt had been established at all. Which was arrested, I did not give any resistance, either passive or active resistance, but I was brutally beaten on the occasion and I have lasting consequences of those beatings. My head was bashed in. Two vertebrae were damaged. I bled from my mouth. I have a scar on the right-hand side of my face from being kicked in the face with a boot and from the beatings I received to my head I have suffered much pain and injury. And I was especially afraid of an automatic rifle that was cocked at my head. I still suffer severe headaches which I did not have previously. I lost my sight. My blood pressure is very high. My capillaries have burst and I have generally undergone stress. This is the basic human rights so I would like to asked what international conventions they adhered to in their conduct. My wife was with me when I was arrested and she suffers permanent consequences as well as my driver who received serious bodily harm, and he took SFOR to Court and received money as remuneration. I am constantly under the care and attention of doctors. I have to take six pills a day. The doctors are attending to my health situation. I went to the Bronovo hospital for several medical examinations, and I was treated in the hospital detention facility for my health problems. I was -- my health was critically jeopardised, and for a time I was not able to attend the court hearings. My health situation has deteriorated of late, and this can be seen from the medical documents. They support that. I suffer from a very serious illness as the doctors have told me, and I don't know what the outcome of that will be. So I'm asking you now, Your Honours, is anybody responsible for that kind of conduct? Will they be held responsible and accountable? According to Article 7(1) I was charged with individual criminal responsibility. All the relevant evidence that the Prosecution has I would like to ask you to scrutinise during your appeals proceedings, and I don't think they prove that I took part directly or indirectly in any act of torture, persecution on political or any other grounds or any other criminal acts at all which are prohibited by the Geneva Conventions. I am ready to accept all responsibility if they are proved true. My active participation in the system of repression does not exist. I did not take part in it and it has not been proved. Just a few more moments, if I may, with the Court's indulgence. Yesterday's statement by the Prosecutor Mr. Carmona with respect to my testimony to the investigators after my arrest. Yes, it is true that I was afraid at the time. I was terribly frightened. Not of my own responsibility or because of any guilt on my part. I was terrified by what I was put through when I was arrested, the injuries I received then and inflicted on me by SFOR. Mr. Carmona, I resisted all evil and the evil in -- that was present in the Investigation Centre of Omarska. I received threats from the Serbs. They said I was helping the Muslims. I did what I could to make life better in the centre of Omarska, and in that respect things have been ascribed to me that I never did. Just a few more words, if I may. For everything that I have said for so far, I question the judgement. I refute all the charges because it was not proved that I committed these acts, and I would like to ask the Appeals Chamber to determine the identity between the indictment and the judgement, to establish the links and to establish the truth and to acquit me and to set me free from further serving my sentence. I state here and now that it is a crime to convict an innocent man and that there is no more terrible sentence than a sentence proclaimed to an innocent man. Justice and the truth, Your Honours, I think, will prevail, and it can be established, and it is up to you to do so. I should like to thank the Appeals Chamber for their understanding and for allowing me to take part in the -- my appellant's brief and to present my own arguments before Your Honours. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mr. Prcac. Thank you very much, Mr. Prcac. Now Mr. Zigic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you like to address the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, just a moment, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Just on a point of order. Without compounding the error, about 120 lines up a mention was made of a witness, a Prosecution's witness and this has to be redacted, and apart from that there was also reference to another Prosecution witness which in fact of course -- who is protected and this would have to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, will you put that in hand.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It will be done. Yes, Mr. Zigic. THE APPELLANT ZIGIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If I keep to your schedule, I only have seven minutes, that's why I would ask you to allow me to speak for another ten minutes, because I believe that what I have to say will take at least 17 minutes, and I would be very grateful if you would permit me to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zigic, how many minutes in all would that make? How many minutes in all would you be wanting? THE APPELLANT ZIGIC: [Interpretation] I apologise in advance, but since my case and the indictment referring to me are very voluminous, I will not be requiring more than 17 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That's far too much, though. What about making that 12 minutes? The Court is prepared to give you 12 minutes. Normally that's almost double the original estimate. THE APPELLANT ZIGIC: [Interpretation] Of course I accept your proposal, Your Honour, but I would like to ask the interpreters then to skip item number 4 so that we would save on time. In any case, I thank you very much. It's very difficult to bear the burden of my first instance conviction during the first instance proceedings. Unfortunately, the Prosecution did not make one single step in order to determine the truth and discover the true perpetrators of the crimes of which I have been convicted. My defence tried several times to clarify some counts of my indictment but did not find understanding on the side of the Prosecution. The Prosecution brought a large number of witnesses who testified on scores of killings in Keraterm and Omarska. Unfortunately, to my detriment many killings were not cleared up to this very day. I apologise for being so free, but I believe that the Prosecution followed the line of least resistance, or they used the system well. Zigic is here, so we will ascribe some killings to him because the others are not accessible to us. I ask myself, is this justice? In this way, we did not establish the truth. The true perpetrators of these crimes were not discovered, some of whom are still walking around Prijedor today, and they are free. In all of this, I fared the worst. I was convicted of crimes which were committed by other people. However, what is even worse is that the Prosecution has available a lot of evidence which clearly says who those people are. Quite to the contrary, and we were assured of this yesterday, how the Prosecution is trying to construe the theory of the killing of Drago Tokmadzic with two beatings and no witness before this Chamber testified on this matter. And further, the Prosecution had access to all commanders of the Security Service as well as the shift leaders from Keraterm and Omarska. The Prosecution did not call any of them to testify of -- about the events from 1992. It is quite clear that these people know who committed the crimes in Keraterm and Omarska. It is quite clear that the three shift leaders covered 24 hours in the camps, and it is clear that some of them or all three of them know what happened. I think that the Prosecution should have called in these eight people to speak about this matter. However, this was not in the interest of the Prosecution, because on several occasions the Prosecution has shown here that they do not care much for the truth. I must tell the Appeals Chamber that the shift leaders and the commanders from the Keraterm camp agreed to testify, but this was prevented by the Prosecution. Kolundzija Dragan, Damir Dosen, and Dusko Sikirica are who have already been convicted had agreed to testify about the events in Keraterm. In the meantime, they made a plea bargain with the Prosecution. The accused Kolundzija Dragan told me personally in the UN Detention Unit that the Prosecution expressly demanded in the plea bargain that they cannot testify. Kolundzija expressed regret but said that he simply did not dare to appear as a witness. What else could I do than give up on counting on him as a witness? But I believe that it is never too late to establish the truth. So I ask the Appeals Chamber to call all the shift leaders and their commanders so that they can testify about the events in the Omarska and Keraterm camps. I should like to mention that in the first instance court proceedings, I could -- I only had Prosecution witnesses, and that is the case today in the appeals process. It is a terrible for me that in addition to having to prove that I did not commit certain crimes for which I have been charged and convicted of I must prove who the perpetrators of those crimes were. I am not in a position to prove that and show that personally. All I can do is through Prosecution witnesses, and this right has been withheld. What I can do today is to offer the Appeals Chamber the Prosecution witnesses who are appear of the circumstances surrounding the killing of Becir Medunjanin. The Prosecution has supplied me with their written statements, and Your Honours, I have eight Prosecution witnesses testifying to Becir Medunjanin's killing. Some of these statements were supplied by the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 68 during the trial itself at the first instance, and other documents were disclosed to me pursuant to Rule 68 once again after the judgement. The Prosecution witnesses who have already testified before this Trial Chamber are Oklopcic Azedin and Abdulah Brkic. The Prosecution witnesses that my Defence asked for -- asked to testify before the Court and the Trial Chamber are the following. (redacted) (redacted) from the Tadic case, and a witness from the Tadic case which was Exhibit 212 in the Kvocka case. We also have another witness, (redacted) (redacted), who is inaccessible to us today. Pursuant to Rule 115, my Defence team handed in two statements in my second brief pursuant to Rule 115. They are D2 and D3, those exhibits. The first of these five witnesses were on the list of Prosecution witnesses. The Prosecution called just two and gave up on the rest. All eight of these witnesses mentioned testified to Becir Medunjanin's killing. They say quite clearly who perpetrated the killing. All of those eight Prosecution witnesses testified about the same individuals as having been the perpetrators of that crime. None of those eight witnesses mention Zoran Zigic although all of them know me. They testify about certain other incidents that took place and linked to me. So I appeal to the Appeals Chamber to invest all its efforts to focus on those crucial testimonies. Furthermore, I should like to appeal to the Prosecution to reinvestigate all its evidence and to raise the indictment against the real perpetrators, those who committed the crimes I have been convicted of. Let me just give an example of the -- where the Prosecution erred. The Prosecution struck from its indictment a man called Goran Lajic who quite obviously killed Drago Tokmadzic as is stated in the judgement itself. The conclusion is quite clear. By striking Goran Lajic from the indictment, the Prosecution committed a fatal error. But, having done so, it tries to put it right by putting forward a false witness, Edin Ganic, who alleged that I was responsible for the death of Drago Tokmadzic. Now, can the Prosecution raise the indictment again? I don't know. All I do know is that all legal and human norms are being violated and that I was convicted for crimes over people did. Your Honours, since the Trial Chamber completely ignored my apologies, sincere apologies to all the victims that had suffered in that unfortunate war, I would like once again to state quite clearly how I have felt throughout all these years, my deepest sentiments. I profoundly apologise to all victims who have been crimes committed against them during the war. I should sincerely like to apologise to the people towards I might have made a mistake or contributed to their sufferings in any way. I have come before this Tribunal of my own free will. I have come to be punished for my sins, the sins of 1992. As to my sincere regrets and apologies to all the victims, I spoke about this before the Trial Chamber pursuant to Rule 84 bis. However, the Trial Chamber in its judgement of the first instance ignored my sincere apologies and remorse, and it relates to what I said pursuant to Rule 84 bis, only in the passage where I am to be convicted and found guilty without mentioning that my statements were given not under a solemn declaration. However, where my defence relates to my statement pursuant to Rule 84 bis, the Trial Chamber has ignored and states that it was not given under the solemn declaration. This is just a small example. There are many more significant examples of things that took place during my trial, and attorney Mr. Stojanovic spoke at length about this and set all this out in my appellant's brief. Your Honours, thank you for your patience and indulgence, and I sincerely hope that what I have said will lead to a positive reaction on the part of the Prosecution and that the Prosecution will do its utmost to bring the real perpetrators to justice. It is never too late to have justice prevail. Thank you, Your Honours, for all the patience you have shown me, and thank you in advance for all the efforts you're going to invest in your deliberations in order to bring in the right decision on appeal. I should like to take advantage of this occasion to tender a document at the request of my lawyer, Mr. Stojanovic. I should like to present it to the registry, hand it over to the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I must tell you this, that this is a procedure intended to enable the appellants to speak directly to the Court. It's not a procedure intended to reargue, for you to reargue your case. You've got very able counsel to do that. All the evidence, all the material such as the material in your hands, has already been presented to the Court. It forms part of the record with the Court. The Court will consider all the material. You need not trouble at this stage to present any further evidence. You can just speak, and we will listen. Mr. Stojanovic. THE APPELLANT ZIGIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to thank you very much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Stojanovic, yes. I ask you to take your seat while we listen to your client. THE APPELLANT ZIGIC: [Interpretation] Once again, thank you very much for that explanation. This is not a document from the case itself. It is, in fact, an opinion given by the head of the Detention Unit as to my conduct during the past six years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, all the documentary material has already been presented in the case, and we have to consider the material. If new material is to be now presented, the other side has to see it and has to be afforded an opportunity to comment on it. We cannot do that. THE APPELLANT ZIGIC: [Interpretation] Then, Your Honour, that was an omission by my lawyer. It is quite simply an opinion given by the head of the Detention Unit with respect to my conduct over the past six years. I don't see that the Prosecution should have anything against this, and I will of course let them see this document. It was given to me by the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Mr. Prosecutor, do you have any objections at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: The Prosecution is put in a rather unenvious position of not knowing what the document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm afraid the Bench is against the admission of this new document. Okay. THE APPELLANT ZIGIC: [Interpretation] I accept your ruling, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now the Court has come to the end of the arguments in the case. The Court has to consider what it will do about the additional evidence matter which came to our notice a while ago, and that we propose to do is to make a Scheduling Order in due course relating to that question, and in that Scheduling Order we will also stipulate the procedure which we intend to follow. That is to say, if and when it becomes necessary to do so. Now, subject to that, I think it remains only for me to thank the parties and counsel on each side for the assistance they have given to the Court and for the professionalism with which they have done their work and the courtesy that they've shown to each other. Whatever happened in the past is a different matter. That, as we say, is history. I would also include in my expresses of appreciation a reference to the registry and to our own staff and to the interpreters. We owe such a great deal to the interpreters, do we not. So we thank them very fulsomely. Now, before the Court retires to consider its verdict which will be announced in due course, I would like to make a reference to Mr. Carmona. I believe that this is his last case. Is that right, Mr. Carmona?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Word has come to the Bench that he's about to leave the institution, and I would like to, on behalf of the Bench, to express our appreciation for the forcefulness of his advocacy and the efficiency with which he has done his work, and we are quite confident that he will take his experience with him to the new position to which he is going in his own country. For the rest, I give him good wishes. And I'm sure I speak for all members of the bar on both sides as well, in addition, of course, to speaking for my colleagues. So now --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: I'm forever grateful, and if I may in fact respond in kind. I must indicate to this learned Tribunal and my colleagues that it has been an immense pleasure. I have in fact appeared in the main before in fact Judge Guney, Judge Pocar and myself, and it is my first appearance before the other two esteemed Judges. And I must in fact admit not only in fact have I learnt a lot, but I have in fact been quite impressed with the after comity, the civility and affability, and most of all the justice with which this Court has conducted its affairs. And I say thank you very much. And if I may be a bit little subjective in relation to you, Judge the President, I can assure you that we in fact in the Caribbean diaspora hold you in very high regard and we wish you all the best also. And to the best of the Bench, all the best. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well now, on that note, the Court will withdraw to consider its verdict of which you will be notified in due course. So the Court now stands adjourned sine die.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: sine die

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.40 p.m.
